_readme: Taxonomy of scam edge cases in Solana transactions. Each entry: what the wallet popup shows (shows), why it is hard to judge (trick), the matching detector rules (rules), what evidence is needed to see it (evidence: free = visible in the popup; simulation / addresses / programs / domain = the four paid checks), and the correct answer (truth: scam / safe / depends). The question bank questions.json references these ids via its case field; npm run coverage lists cases that have no question yet.

categories.A: Authority & permissions: money can leave without a Transfer
categories.B: Transfers & recipients: where the money actually goes
categories.C: Signatures & transaction structure: the parts you cannot see
categories.D: Programs & contracts: what is being called
categories.E: Domains & frontends: where it came from
categories.F: Airdrops / NFTs / minting: you expect to receive, you end up giving
categories.G: Tokens & trades: the transaction is fine, the asset is the trap
categories.H: Fees & resources: drained without a transfer instruction
categories.I: Language & context: the copy itself is a signal
categories.J: False positives: looks scary, actually normal

cases.name: Unlimited approval
cases.shows: Approve / ApproveChecked with the u64 max amount (18446744073709551615); the wallet may show it as “unlimited” or a long string of digits
cases.trick: The copy says “claim / sign in” but the instruction is an approval; many people do not know approve ≠ transfer

cases.name: Bounded amount, but delegated to a stranger
cases.shows: Approve amount exactly equals your full balance, and the delegate is a plain wallet, not a program
cases.trick: The amount looks “reasonable” and slips past checks that only watch for unlimited approvals; look at who the delegate is

cases.name: Change token account ownership
cases.shows: SetAuthority with authorityType = AccountOwner and a new owner that is someone else
cases.trick: “Set authority” sounds like configuration, not moving money; the effect is handing over the account together with its balance

cases.name: Close authority on a wSOL account
cases.shows: SetAuthority with authorityType = CloseAccount on your wSOL account
cases.trick: Money can be taken without changing the owner: when a wSOL account is closed, its lamports go to whoever closes it

cases.name: System Assign changes the wallet owner
cases.shows: A System Program Assign that sets your wallet account's owner to some program
cases.trick: Very rare and wallets barely explain it; once signed, the whole account is controlled by the program

cases.name: Stake authority transfer
cases.shows: A Stake Program Authorize that hands Staker / Withdrawer to someone else, framed as “migrate to a higher-yield validator”
cases.trick: The staked balance looks untouched, but the authority is no longer yours

cases.name: Nonce account authority transfer
cases.shows: AuthorizeNonceAccount hands the nonce authority to someone else
cases.trick: Harmless on its own; combined with a durable nonce, the other party can broadcast a transaction for you at any time

cases.name: Approval hidden in a CPI
cases.shows: The popup shows a single call to some program; the approval happens inside the program via CPI
cases.trick: The instruction list is spotless; only simulation shows the delegate changed

cases.name: “Revoke” tool that approves instead
cases.shows: The button says Revoke, but the instruction is an Approve to the tool itself
cases.trick: Name and content are opposites; it exploits your security instinct to “clean up approvals”

cases.name: Token-2022 permanent delegate
cases.shows: A normal token purchase, but the token you receive carries the permanentDelegate extension
cases.trick: The transaction itself has no red flags; the issuer can pull the tokens out at any time later

cases.name: Address poisoning (same prefix/suffix as a contact)
cases.shows: The recipient shares the first and last 4 characters with an address book entry but differs in the middle
cases.trick: Wallets and explorers show only the first and last few characters; the fake address is sitting right in your history

cases.name: Poisoned address copied from history
cases.shows: The recipient was copied from the “previous” transaction in history and is not in the address book
cases.trick: No address book entry to compare against, so the free view cannot catch it; address reputation shows it dusting everyone

cases.name: Transfer smuggled into a swap
cases.shows: An 8-instruction swap with a System Transfer to the dapp's address mixed in, labelled “network fee”
cases.trick: Buried in a pile of instructions, and the amount is 98% of your SOL balance

cases.name: Excessive platform fee
cases.shows: A swap with a transfer to the platform fee account worth 20% of the trade
cases.trick: A small platform fee (around 0.1%) is normal; the line is the ratio

cases.name: “Free mint” that transfers your NFT away
cases.shows: TransferChecked with amount = 1, where the mint is a valuable NFT in your wallet
cases.trick: An amount of 1 looks harmless; it is actually an entire NFT leaving

cases.name: Creating an ATA before sending USDC to a new address
cases.shows: Two instructions, CreateAssociatedTokenAccount + TransferChecked, plus 0.002 SOL of extra rent
cases.trick: “One extra instruction and a bit more SOL” is easily mistaken for foul play

cases.name: Closing the wSOL account after a swap
cases.shows: CloseAccount with destination = yourself
cases.trick: “Close account” sounds scary; refunding to yourself is just a normal unwrap

cases.name: Durable nonce disguised as signature verification
cases.shows: “Sign to verify your wallet”; the transaction starts with AdvanceNonceAccount and wallet simulation fails
cases.trick: Nothing happens after you sign; the other party can broadcast days later. Normal transactions expire in 2 minutes, durable nonce ones do not

cases.name: “Message” bytes that are really a transaction
cases.shows: You are asked to sign a message whose bytes deserialize into a valid transaction
cases.trick: If the wallet does not block it, signing the message is signing the transaction

cases.name: “Free” transaction where they pay the gas
cases.shows: The fee payer is not you, you are only a co-signer; but the instruction's sender is you
cases.trick: “0 fee, sponsored” makes you relax; a co-signature is still a signature

cases.name: Address hidden in a Lookup Table
cases.shows: A versioned transaction references an Address Lookup Table; the wallet cannot resolve the delegate / recipient and shows “unknown account”
cases.trick: The key address is invisible; only simulation can resolve it, and then you check its reputation

cases.name: Deliberately failing wallet simulation
cases.shows: The wallet says “cannot preview balance changes”
cases.trick: Normal transactions occasionally fail simulation too (expired blockhash, balance edge cases); this alone does not convict

cases.name: Payload smuggled into a multisig co-signature
cases.shows: Someone else's multisig transaction asks for your co-signature, and one of its instructions has you as the authority
cases.trick: On the surface it is someone else's transaction; your signature is what makes that one instruction valid

cases.name: SIWS plaintext sign-in
cases.shows: A Sign-In With Solana plaintext message with domain / nonce / issuedAt all present
cases.trick: Plaintext signatures are generally harmless; check that the domain in the message matches the page's domain

cases.name: Two steps: create the nonce account first
cases.shows: The first transaction just creates a nonce account (harmless); the second one uses it
cases.trick: The first transaction alone looks fine; ask “why does a login page want me to create a nonce account”

cases.name: Everything at once (drainer kit)
cases.shows: Approve + Transfer + SetAuthority + CloseAccount crammed into one transaction
cases.trick: Not subtle, but real drainers do exactly this; too many instructions to bother reading

cases.name: Newly deployed unverified program
cases.shows: A call to a program deployed 3 days ago, unverified, with a hot wallet as upgrade authority
cases.trick: A program can be named anything; the popup shows whatever label the dapp supplies

cases.name: Program ID lookalike
cases.shows: The program ID starts like Jupiter's (JUP6Lkb…) and the label says Jupiter
cases.trick: Wallets show names by prefix; an agent that compares the full ID against the official one it knows can catch this for free

cases.name: Upgradeable but multisig-controlled legitimate program
cases.shows: The program check shows upgradeable = true
cases.trick: “Upgradeable” gets read as a risk; what matters is whether the upgrade authority is a multisig / DAO or a hot wallet

cases.name: Clean outer call, inner CPI moves tokens out
cases.shows: A single call to an unfamiliar program with your token account in the account list
cases.trick: The transfer happens inside the program; there is no Transfer in the instruction list, but simulation shows the balance change

cases.name: Official domain hijacked / poisoned frontend
cases.shows: The domain is the real jup.ag, but the transaction approves a drainer
cases.trick: The domain check is all green; the lesson is “right domain ≠ right transaction”, the instructions decide in the end

cases.name: Legitimate program, legitimate domain, tampered parameter
cases.shows: A Jupiter route with minOut = 0
cases.trick: Everything is “green” except the slippage parameter; sandwich bots will eat most of it

cases.name: Typo / brand-word domain
cases.shows: jup-airdrop.xyz, orca-swap.finance, revoke-cash-sol.com
cases.trick: Containing the brand name makes you relax; registered only days ago

cases.name: Homoglyph domain
cases.shows: jυp.ag (Greek letter υ)
cases.trick: Nearly indistinguishable by eye; the free check is whether the domain contains non-ASCII characters

cases.name: Subdomain trick
cases.shows: jup.ag.swap-app.com
cases.trick: Seeing the official domain at the start makes you relax; the real root domain is swap-app.com

cases.name: Freshly registered domain
cases.shows: Registered 5 days ago, certificate just issued
cases.trick: No history does not mean scam, but it weighs heavily when stacked with other signals

cases.name: Official secondary domain / app subdomain
cases.shows: app.drift.trade
cases.trick: Not being on “the list I know” does not make it fake; domain verification confirms who owns it

cases.name: Fake link posted by official social media
cases.shows: A Discord / X announcement linking to a mint site
cases.trick: A trusted source does not make the target trusted (social accounts get hacked)

cases.name: “Claim airdrop” that is really an approval
cases.shows: Button says Claim; instruction is Approve / SetAuthority
cases.trick: You expect to receive, you end up granting authority; a label that contradicts the instruction type is visible for free

cases.name: Airdropped NFT with a phishing link in its metadata
cases.shows: A new NFT appears in your wallet; the image says “go to xxx.xyz to claim your prize”
cases.trick: The NFT itself is harmless, the link is the danger; these questions are framed as “should you go sign at the link”

cases.name: “Burn spam NFT for a reward” with an authority change attached
cases.shows: A BurnChecked followed by a SetAuthority
cases.trick: The burn itself is safe; the instruction after it is the real purpose

cases.name: Cleaning up spam NFTs yourself
cases.shows: BurnChecked + CloseAccount with destination = yourself
cases.trick: Both “burn” and “close” sound scary; refunding to yourself is just normal cleanup

cases.name: Pay and receive nothing
cases.shows: The “mint” is a single SOL Transfer to a plain address, with no mint instruction at all
cases.trick: The free view shows “no mint instruction”; simulation confirms outflow only; address reputation confirms it is a rug

cases.name: Page price does not match the transaction amount
cases.shows: The page says 0.1 SOL; the transaction transfers 1 SOL
cases.trick: Just one decimal point off; compare the number in the copy with the number in the instruction

cases.name: Fake token with the same symbol
cases.shows: The “USDC” received from the swap is a different mint
cases.trick: Same symbol; check whether the mint you receive is the official one

cases.name: Freeze authority honeypot
cases.shows: The token you buy has a hot wallet as freezeAuthority
cases.trick: Buying works perfectly; your account gets frozen when you try to sell

cases.name: Mint authority not renounced
cases.shows: mintAuthority is still set
cases.trick: A long-term risk, not a transaction risk; on its own it is medium

cases.name: Transfer hook that rejects transfers out
cases.shows: A Token-2022 token with the transferHook extension
cases.trick: The hook program can reject every outgoing transfer, which means you cannot sell

cases.name: Zero slippage protection
cases.shows: A legitimate route with minOut = 0
cases.trick: The frontend or a browser extension changed the slippage; see D6

cases.name: Complex but normal route
cases.shows: A 3-pool Jupiter route with 9 instructions, including ATA create / close and compute budget
cases.trick: Many instructions get misjudged; every instruction's recipient is yourself or a program

cases.name: Bounded approval to a verified program
cases.shows: Approve amount equals the trade amount, the delegate is the program authority, and there is a Revoke at the end
cases.trick: The word “approve”; bounded amount + program authority + revoke afterwards is the standard pattern

cases.name: Priority fee drain
cases.shows: An absurd SetComputeUnitPrice, 7 SOL in fees; no transfer instruction at all
cases.trick: SOL burned with no “transfer”; compute the fee as units × microLamports

cases.name: Rent drain
cases.shows: Dozens of accounts created at once, several SOL of rent in total, and the other party can close the accounts
cases.trick: Each account is small money; the total is not

cases.name: Normal priority fee
cases.shows: SetComputeUnitPrice of a few hundred microLamports, 0.0001 SOL in fees
cases.trick: A compute budget instruction is not a risk in itself

cases.name: Urgency language
cases.shows: “Verify within 10 minutes or your wallet will be frozen”
cases.trick: Copy is a weak signal that does not convict on its own, but it lowers your tolerance for other signals

cases.name: “Support” DM asking you to sign a verification transaction
cases.shows: The channel is a DM; the transaction is a durable nonce or an approval
cases.trick: Legitimate projects never DM you to sign anything

cases.name: Transfer requested by an address book contact
cases.shows: The address exactly matches the address book
cases.trick: Normal; the difference from poisoning is that “exact” match

cases.name: Normal transaction that fails simulation
cases.shows: An ordinary Jupiter swap where wallet simulation fails (expired blockhash)
cases.trick: A failed simulation on its own is only low; re-simulating shows the normal balance changes

cases.name: Ordinary transfer with a memo
cases.shows: Transfer + Memo (“rent”) + one compute budget instruction
cases.trick: Not recognizing the Memo program makes it look like an unfamiliar program

cases.name: A real Revoke
cases.shows: A Revoke instruction with no Approve
cases.trick: The difference from A9: here the type really is Revoke
